content: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously grouped under non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), is a leading cause of liver fat accumulation driven by metabolic dysfunction. MASLD is characterized by excessive fat deposition in liver cells not attributed to significant alcohol intake. It is strongly associated with insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and components of metabolic syndrome. The disease spectrum ranges from simple steatosis (fat accumulation) to advanced conditions such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), fibrosis, and cirrhosis. MASLD pathophysiology involves complex mechanisms including insulin resistance promoting hepatic lipogenesis, oxidative stress, inflammatory cytokines, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Diagnosis typically centers on elevated liver enzymes and imaging studies such as ultrasound or transient elastography, sometimes requiring biopsy for severity assessment. Management primarily focuses on lifestyle modifications—healthy diet, weight loss, and physical activity—that improve metabolic health and reduce liver fat. Limited pharmacological options exist, with ongoing research into treatments targeting metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Important practical considerations include monitoring for disease progression and cardiovascular risks. Safety issues involve avoiding alcohol and hepatotoxic medications. MASLD terminology reflects evolving understanding, distinguishing it from alcohol-related liver disease or viral hepatitis. Limitations in current knowledge include variability in disease progression and response to interventions. This educational module helps consumers and healthcare providers understand MASLD’s causes, diagnosis, management, and myths, supporting informed health decisions and improved liver outcomes.

content: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is an umbrella term describing liver fat accumulation related to metabolic dysfunction. It replaces the older term non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) to emphasize its association with metabolic abnormalities rather than solely alcohol intake. MASLD includes a spectrum from simple steatosis—where fat accumulates without inflammation—to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), where inflammation and liver cell damage occur. Recognizing this terminology shift helps healthcare providers tailor diagnosis and management around metabolic health.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: The primary cause of MASLD is metabolic dysfunction, often characterized by insulin resistance. Insulin resistance promotes increased fat synthesis in liver cells and decreased fat breakdown, leading to triglyceride accumulation. Oxidative stress from excess fat triggers inflammatory pathways and mitochondrial impairment, contributing to liver injury. Genetics, gut microbiota, and diet also influence MASLD development. Understanding these mechanisms is vital to grasp why managing metabolic risk factors can prevent or reverse MASLD.

content: Key risk factors include overweight or obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia (abnormal blood cholesterol and triglycerides), metabolic syndrome, sedentary lifestyle, poor diet high in saturated fats or sugars, and older age. Family history and certain ethnic backgrounds increase susceptibility. Awareness of these factors allows for early screening and intervention to minimize liver damage and systemic complications.

content: Many people with MASLD are asymptomatic in early stages. When symptoms occur, they may include fatigue, mild right upper abdominal discomfort, or nonspecific symptoms like malaise. Advanced disease may show signs of liver dysfunction such as jaundice, swelling, or cognitive impairment from hepatic encephalopathy. Because symptoms are often subtle or absent, routine screening in high-risk individuals is important.

content: Doctors diagnose MASLD using clinical evaluation, blood tests, and imaging. Liver enzymes such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are often elevated, but can be normal. Ultrasound can detect liver fat but not inflammation or fibrosis. Advanced imaging like transient elastography estimates liver stiffness to assess fibrosis. Liver biopsy remains the gold standard to distinguish steatosis from steatohepatitis and fibrosis in uncertain cases. Diagnosis integrates clinical context, labs, and imaging findings.

content: Currently, no FDA-approved medications specifically treat MASLD; management focuses on controlling metabolic risk factors. Weight loss of 7-10% body weight can reduce liver fat and inflammation. Lifestyle modifications include adopting a Mediterranean or balanced diet low in saturated fats and simple sugars and engaging in moderate-intensity physical activity for 150 minutes weekly. Control of diabetes, lipid levels, and hypertension is integral. Some medications under investigation target insulin resistance and inflammation but require further evidence.

content: Healthy lifestyle behaviors effectively prevent and improve MASLD. Nutritional strategies emphasize whole grains, fruits, vegetables, lean protein, and healthy fats while minimizing processed foods and fructose-containing beverages. Regular exercise enhances insulin sensitivity and reduces fat accumulation. Avoiding alcohol is recommended even though MASLD is non-alcoholic, as alcohol may exacerbate liver injury. Sustainable lifestyle changes should be individualized and supported by healthcare professionals.

Risk stratification tools and regular monitoring help detect worsening liver disease.

content: Misconceptions include that fatty liver disease only affects people who drink alcohol or that it always causes obvious symptoms. Some believe MASLD is irreversible or unimportant, which is not true—early lifestyle intervention can reverse or stabilize disease. Dispelling these misconceptions encourages proactive health behaviors and better disease outcomes.

chunk_title: The Role of Weight Loss and Exercise in MASLD
content: Weight loss is the cornerstone of MASLD management. A sustained reduction of 7-10% can lead to significant improvements in liver fat, inflammation, and fibrosis. Exercise independently improves insulin sensitivity and hepatic metabolism even without large weight loss. Both aerobic and resistance training show benefits. Combining dietary changes with physical activity yields the best outcomes. These strategies also improve cardiovascular health and overall quality of life.
